segments.english: As for you, take for yourself some of every kind of food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself, so that it will be food for you and for them.
segments.literal: and-you take-(imperative) to-you from-all-of food that is-eaten and-you-shall-gather to-you and-it-shall-be to-you and-to-them for-food

tokens.note: imperative; the maqqef joins it to the next word
weqatal after an imperative: a sequential command

phrases.literal: 'and-you': the fronted independent pronoun sets Noah against the doomed world

phrases.english: some of every kind of food
phrases.literal: 'from-all-of food': partitive מִן, 'some of every food'
'and-you-shall-gather to-you'; the object is the food, implied

phrases.english: so that it will be food for you and for them
phrases.literal: 'and-it-shall-be to-you and-to-them for-food'; the weqatal gives purpose or result

grammar: וְאַתָּה begins with an independent pronoun, which contrasts Noah with everyone else.
קַח is an imperative; וְאָסַפְתָּ is a weqatal continuing the command.
The etnaḥta on אֵלֶיךָ divides the verse: the gathering, then the purpose.
לְאָכְלָה is a feminine noun 'food' with prefixed ל, giving 'as food'.
segments.note: The 'them' of the last clause are the animals of 6:19-20; Radak says even the predators ate the same plant foods, as before the creation of meat-eating.

commentary.summary: Radak: since the animals come to Noah to be kept alive, he must prepare food for himself and for them; the food is fruits, seeds and plants, and even predators eat them.
Sforno: now take various foods for the various kinds; it adds detail, not a different reading.
Onkelos renders the verse closely: 'take for yourself of all food that is eaten and gather it to you, and it shall be for you and for them to eat'.

segments.english: Noah did so; just as God had commanded him, so he did.
segments.literal: and-did Noah like-all that commanded him God so he-did

phrases.english: just as God had commanded him
phrases.literal: 'like-all that commanded him God'; כֹּל is idiomatic: 'exactly as'
'so he-did': repeats the verb as a summary

grammar: The wayyiqtol וַיַּעַשׂ narrates; the closing כֵּן עָשָׂה is a qatal that summarizes.
The telisha gedola on כְּכֹל marks a long disjunctive-like prepositive accent.
אֹתוֹ is the object marker with a 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'him'.
The Hebrew states obedience twice, before and after the commandment.
segments.note: The English line moves the clause 'so he did' to the end, as the Hebrew does. Ramban: the double statement shows that he left nothing out of what he was commanded.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'this is the building of the ark': the making that Noah did is the construction of the ark.
Ramban: Noah both built the ark and gathered the food; the repetition 'so he did' shows he omitted nothing.
Radak: he made the ark exactly as commanded, in length, width, height, nests, and the food he put in it.
Onkelos: 'and Noah did according to all that the LORD commanded him; so he did'.

apparatus: Onkelos has יְיָ ('the LORD') for אֱלֹהִים; this is Targum Onkelos's rendering, not a variant of the Hebrew.

segments.english: Then the LORD said to Noah: Come, you and all your household, into the ark, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation.
segments.literal: and-said the-LORD to-Noah come-(imperative) you and-all-of house-your to the-ark for you-(object) I-saw righteous before-me in-the-generation the-this

tokens.note: imperative of בוא; a weak (hollow) root
the object marker with suffix is placed first for emphasis

phrases.english: Then the LORD said to Noah
Come, you and all your household, into the ark
I have seen that you are righteous
phrases.literal: 'you I-saw righteous': the object אֹתְךָ is fronted

grammar: אֹתְךָ is the object marker with a suffix, fronted before the verb; it stresses 'you, and no one else'.
בֹּא־אַתָּה uses an independent pronoun after the imperative for emphasis.
The etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה separates the command from its reason.
צַדִּיק is the predicate of the object: 'I saw you (as) righteous'.
segments.note: Rashi stresses that the text says only 'righteous', not 'righteous and blameless' as in 6:9: a person is praised in part to his face, in full behind his back. Ramban and Sforno hold the emphatic 'you' implies that the household is saved for his sake only. The English keeps 'you' plain; the emphasis goes in the notes.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the verse does not say 'righteous and blameless'; one says part of a man's praise in his presence and all of it in his absence (Genesis Rabbah). The English says only 'righteous'.
Ramban: Noah is told to enter with his whole household, and the text shows that they are saved in his merit alone, since it does not say 'I have seen you all righteous'.
Sforno: 'you, not your house' (the household is saved only because of him).
Radak: it is fitting that you and all your household escape the flood so that the world is settled again.
Onkelos: 'enter, you and all the people of your house, into the ark, for I have seen you righteous (zakkai) before me in this generation'.

segments.english: Of every clean animal take for yourself seven each, a male and his mate; and of the animals that are not clean, two, a male and his mate.
segments.literal: from-all-of the-animal the-clean you-shall-take to-you seven seven man and-his-wife and-from the-animal that not clean it two man and-his-wife

tokens.note: yiqtol with the force of a command
repeated number: distributive, 'seven each' or 'seven by seven'
literally 'man'; used of animals: 'one of a pair'
the pronoun repeats the subject: 'that is not clean'

phrases.literal: 'from-all-of the-animal the-clean'; the ו of the second half and the construct make 'from every'
'you-shall-take to-you'; an imperfect used as command
'man and-his-wife': the Hebrew uses the human terms of animals
'which not clean it': the negative expresses the absence of the quality

grammar: תִּקַּח is an imperfect used as a command; the accent on לְךָ is tevir.
שִׁבְעָה שִׁבְעָה is distributive repetition. It can mean seven individuals of each kind or seven pairs; the text itself says 'a male and his mate' after it.
אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ are the words for a human husband and wife, here applied to animals (Radak: a figurative use).
לֹא טְהֹרָה הִוא ('not clean') is a euphemism for 'unclean' (Radak, and the rabbis: avoid a foul word).
segments.note: The English leaves the ambiguity in 'seven each' (seven individuals or seven pairs). Radak reads seven pairs; Rashi says only that the extras are for a sacrifice at exit. 'Clean' is not defined in the text; Rashi reads it as 'destined to be clean for Israel', Sforno as 'fit for sacrifice', and Radak that God told Noah the signs of cleanness or that he recognized them by their coming in sevens.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'the clean' means those destined to be clean for Israel, and from this we learn that Noah studied Torah; the English takes it as simply 'clean'.
Rashi: the seven each are so that he can offer a sacrifice from them on leaving the ark; it explains 'seven' and does not change the English.
Radak: he says now that Noah should bring seven pairs of each clean animal and one pair (or two) of the unclean; he asks how Noah knew which was clean and gives two answers.
Radak: אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ means male and female, said figuratively; when the pairs are alike the text says 'a woman to her sister', and when they differ as male and female it says 'man and his wife'.
Radak: the text says 'not clean' rather than 'unclean' as it often does, and the rabbis learned from it that one should not speak a foul word.
Sforno: at that time all clean animals were fit for sacrifice, as the rabbis said, and in their food-nature unlike 'you shall be defiled by them'.
Onkelos: 'seven seven, male and female' and 'two, male and female' for the unclean.

segments.english: Also of the birds of the sky, seven each, male and female, to keep seed alive across the face of all the earth.
segments.literal: also from-bird-of the-heavens seven seven male and-female to-keep-alive seed upon face-of all-of the-earth

tokens.note: Piel infinitive construct of חיה: 'to preserve alive'
'offspring'; here, the line of descent for the species

phrases.english: Also of the birds of the sky
phrases.literal: 'also from-bird-of the-heavens'; עוֹף is a collective singular

phrases.english: across the face of all the earth

grammar: עוֹף is a collective singular, so the English plural 'birds'.
שִׁבְעָה שִׁבְעָה is again distributive; here זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה explains it.
לְחַיּוֹת is a Piel infinitive construct and gives the purpose.
The tevir on הַשָּׁמַיִם and the etnaḥta on וּנְקֵבָה mark the verse's two breaks.
segments.note: גַּם ('also') joins the birds to the clean animals of 7:2. Rashi reads the verse as speaking of clean birds only, learning the unstated from the stated; Radak makes the point that the birds came in sevens whether clean or not and discusses it at 7:2.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the verse speaks of clean birds; the unstated case is learned from the stated one. The English 'also of the birds' does not add 'clean'; the note records this.
Radak: 'over the face of all the earth': as at 1:25, the animals' places are divided over the whole earth.
Onkelos: 'also of the birds of the heavens, seven seven, male and female, to preserve seed over all the earth'.

segments.english: For in seven more days I will make it rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from the face of the ground.
segments.literal: for to-days still seven I causing-rain upon the-earth forty day and-forty night and-I-will-wipe-out (object) all-of the-existing-thing that I-made from-upon face-of the-ground

tokens.note: 'to days': after a period, in a span of

tokens.gloss: am about to make it rain

tokens.note: weqatal after the participle: a future act
a rare word, found only in this story (Ibn Ezra); the root is קום or יקם

phrases.literal: 'for to-days still seven': 'after seven more days'

phrases.english: I will make it rain on the earth
phrases.literal: 'I causing-rain upon the-earth': the participle gives the near future

phrases.english: and I will wipe out every living thing
from the face of the ground

grammar: The participle מַמְטִיר expresses what is about to happen; the weqatal וּמָחִיתִי continues it.
יָמִים ... עוֹד שִׁבְעָה: 'still seven days'; the preposition ל marks the span after which the event occurs.
הַיְקוּם is found only here (and 7:23); Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as a general word for every living being.
The verse uses אֲדָמָה (ground), not אֶרֶץ, for what is wiped out.
segments.note: The BDB entry gives `substance, existence` for הַיְקוּם; the English 'living thing' follows Ibn Ezra, 'a general term for every living being on the earth' and Radak ('all that is on the face of the ground among living beings'). Radak adds that it does not include fish or those in the ark. Rashi reads the seven days as the mourning for Methuselah and the 'still' as additional to the 120 years; neither changes the plain translation.

commentary.summary: Rashi: these seven days are the mourning for Methuselah the righteous; God spared his honor and delayed the punishment; count his years and you find they end in the six hundredth year of Noah (Sanhedrin 108). The English gives only 'seven more days'.
Rashi: what is 'still'? Another period after, added to the 120 years.
Rashi: forty days matches the forming of the embryo, since they corrupted themselves; a homily that does not bear on the translation.

Ibn Ezra: on the seventh day it will rain until the end of forty days; this was on the tenth of the second month, and the middle returns to the front, a secret (the text is cut off). He counts the days differently from the plain reading.

Ibn Ezra: הַיְקוּם is found only in this section; its root is among verbs whose first letter is not complete (like כרוב), or among hollow verbs, and it is a general term for every living thing on the ground.
Radak: Noah is to enter the ark seven days before the flood to prepare places and food; the rabbis say the seven days are for Methuselah's mourning.
Radak: הַיְקוּם is general for everything alive on the ground; the root is קום with a letter yod added, as in רִיבָה.
Radak: 'every living thing' means what is on dry land and on the ground, not fish or what is in the ark.
Onkelos: 'for after a time of seven more days I am bringing rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every standing thing that I made from upon the face of the earth'.

apparatus: Onkelos has 'every standing thing' (יְקוּמָא) and 'from upon the face of the earth' (אַרְעָא), reading the last word as 'earth' where the Hebrew has אֲדָמָה.

segments.english: Noah did just as the LORD had commanded him.
segments.literal: and-did Noah like-all that commanded-him the-LORD

tokens.note: Piel perfect with a 3rd masculine suffix

phrases.english: just as the LORD had commanded him
phrases.literal: 'like-all that commanded-him the-LORD'; the Hebrew says 'all' and the English 'just as'

grammar: The narrative wayyiqtol וַיַּעַשׂ begins the report of obedience.
צִוָּהוּ is a Piel perfect with a pronominal suffix.
The divine name here is יְהוָה, where 6:22 had אֱלֹהִים.
The etnaḥta on נֹחַ divides subject from the measure of obedience.
segments.note: The Hebrew repeats the report of 6:22, with the divine name changed. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read 'Noah did' as his entering the ark; Radak the same. The English line gives the plain wording.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'Noah did' means his entering the ark.
Ibn Ezra: as he was commanded, he came with his household close to the ark.
Radak: he entered the ark, he and his household, and brought in the animals, as it says 'and Noah came' (7:7).
Onkelos: 'and Noah did according to all that the LORD commanded him'.

segments.english: Now Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came, water upon the earth.
segments.literal: and-Noah son-of six hundreds year and-the-flood was waters upon the-earth

phrases.english: Now Noah was six hundred years old
phrases.literal: 'and-Noah son-of six hundreds year'; the ו is circumstantial
'waters upon the-earth'; מַבּוּל מַיִם is 'flood of water'

grammar: בֶּן־שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה is the idiom for age: 'son of six hundred years'.
The ו of וְהַמַּבּוּל is circumstantial: 'when' (Radak).
מַיִם is a plural noun 'water'.
The etnaḥta on שָׁנָה divides Noah's age from the flood.
segments.note: Radak takes וְהַמַּבּוּל הָיָה מַיִם as 'the flood of water was', the word 'flood' standing for two (flood, water). The English line reads 'the flood came, water upon the earth'.

commentary.summary: Radak: it tells how old Noah was when he entered the ark because of the flood that was coming.
Radak: the ו means 'when', as in the verses he quotes; Noah was six hundred when the flood came.
Radak: 'flood of water'; the one word 'flood' stands for two.
Onkelos: 'and Noah was a son of six hundred years, and the flood was waters on the earth'.
